Young Farmers [6243]

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Meet four young farmers who speak frankly about the day to day difficulties of farming but are unshaken in their passion and drive. Be it stock theft, climate change and the everyday of toil of working the land, they face these challenges head on. It's back breaking work but it's a calling they choose everyday.

Summary:
Agriculture in South Africa has held out as a strong sector in a unsteady and weak economy. And it outputs are certainly sought after in the world. But the lack of government support and unimaginative policies, this historically white dominated industry, does not necessarily have the appeal for young people as a career choice. But there's a generation of young people, who have mastered their talents in other careers, that is enthusiastic and unphased by the strains of being a farmer in South Africa.

Further information:
South Africa's agriculture sector contributes 2 percent towards the country's GDP and employs over 800 thousand people. It's export driven and a big player globally. However government support is lacking compared to other countries and the bureaucracy can stifle the passion of an emerging farmer, so much so that many have found ways to make it without government support. According to AgriSA economist, funding is a critical problem as it is often linked to land ownership.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel, driving long distances.
Keneilwe's farm is 1h30min away from Randburg, Olerile's is 5hrs away and Thabani is in Mooi River KZN. Hoping to get a local camera guy to shoot his interview.

Script:


Agriculture is a crucial part of our economy. Farmland spans hundreds of thousands of hectares, ensuring food security, much needed export earnings and providing an economic lifeline to many small towns.

Historically dominated by the white community, the sector is undergoing change.
LINK

I’m on the road meeting young black farmers, with grit and passion, they are making inroads into the commercial market.
On a long, flat stretch of road, on the outskirts of the North-West province, we find Amantsi Farm. We’ve arrived at an anxious time: until recently, transporting cattle across provincial borders was banned because of an outbreak of the dreaded foot-and-mouth disease. Our car is disinfected before driving in.
Olerile Lekgetho, left his auditing job to run this 400 ha farm.

He served an apprenticeship of sorts when, as a youngster, he herded his grandfather’s cattle during the school holidays.


Olerile Lekgetho

First of all you need to have the mindset that farming is a business.
His cattle are a long-term investment,
Today he’s disinfecting the cows for ticks. But, it’s the highly contagious foot-and-mouth - a disease caused by a virus - that most concerns him. An outbreak would force him to cull his herd and leave him destitute.

His first cow was a donation from his grandfather.



Olerile
To multiply like this obviously the cow gives birth every year, but also from my salary, I would maybe every third month, save some buy a calf and also when I resigned 04;34 I took all my pensions and put them into cattle.
But it’s not just the threat of disease keeping Olerile awake at night. Stock theft is a near constant threat,


Whilst the SAPS recorded a decrease in stock theft crimes this year, industry insiders claim over 130 000 cases were reported. Setting back the sector over R1 billion.



Olerile
We don’t sleep at all, we’re always on our toes.



Olerile
You’d find somebody’s been caught with cattle that they’ve stolen after two weeks the case is dismissed from the roll in court.
But the rural crimewave isn’t limited to livestock. We travel to southern Gauteng to meet a young farmer fighting to keep her business alive after the theft of her biggest tractor in September.


For Keneilwe Raphesu, the impacts of the theft have been significant..


And to buffer these types of setbacks farmers are forced to turn to credit. With the current commercial agricultural debt estimated at R200 billion, it’s an albatross for both cautious creditors and desperate farmers.

To try balance their books, farmers are constantly trying to increase production. And it’s in the spring months that cattle farmers expect to extend their herd.


Kneilwe
Now we need to find someone to come and plant for us, we need to have the credit to say we’ll pay after harvesting. And after harvesting, you don’t see the profits cause you need to pay people back.

LINK

It’s calving season so twice a day, workers at the farm set out on horseback to see if there’s been any new arrivals. There’s a lot of ground to cover,
It’s an idyllic scene that hides another of the challenges emerging farmers face. This land where Olerile grazes his cattle belongs to the government. He’s leasing it with the option to buy at a later stage.


To buy commercial farming land from the outset would be unaffordable as farming is already capital intensive


Notwithstanding the difficulties, Olerile hopes to leave this land to his daughter. Though just 12, she already owns 3 cows.

Olerile
I’ve sat down with her and discuss that your 3 cattle let’s do a 20year plan,
Like Olerile, Keneilwe’s family leases this 400ha farm from the government. She took over running it from her elderly father

Keneilwe
I’ve managed to improve on, book keeping for instance, my dad would keep a pile of slips and sometimes the writing is worn off and you can’t even see what’s going on,
Many black farmers are raising enough capital in 5 to 10 years to buy the land outright. That’s if all goes according to plan.
Malatu Netshaulu is an agricultural economist at Nedbank


So, the consequences of not owning the land they work are significant for black farmers. And among the reasons land reform has been a slow-burn in South Africa. Since 1994 about 10 percent of commercial farmland has been redistributed to Africans.

It’s hardly an ideal situation in a country where commercial farmers are increasingly exiting the industry.



Malatu
Because of how the sector is set up, because of its history, you’ll find that black farmers, emerging farmers they don’t own the land,


Malatu
The average age of commercial farmers, we’re talking about 60,62 It’s important that you start having these young ones or new people for that matter to come into the sector.


Thabani Bengu is a former professional soccer player. He rents a 45ha mixed crop farm from the community in Mooi River, Kwazulu Natal on condition that he employs the locals.
Thabani

For me farming is practical, lead by example. Go on the field, work with them.



Thabani
What I really enjoy is to watch everything growing step by step.
It’s on Thabani’s farm that we hear of arguably the most unpredictable challenge facing the country’s farmers : climate change! A hail storm in October destroyed his crop but even that paled in comparison to the damage caused by last year’s flooding



Thabani
I planted about 150 thousand crops, you know when you see your crops they are coming okay now, you gonna harvest and make money and all my crops were flooded. It was my downfall but farming is something else, I didn’t give up
LINK
The first rains of the season have fallen, this used to be a good sign for farmers. But considering last year’s heavy rains and unseasonal floods in parts of the country, farmers are anxious about this season’s forecasts and what it could mean for their crops.

Keneilwe

The other parts of the farm we planted soya bean the first time, there was a lot of rain, a lot of water within the soil, we had to replant it and it didn’t come out the way that we wanted to.

This was almost R300 000 washed away in heavy down pours.



These stresses are all too familiar to Thabane. When natural disaster struck his sold his iphone




Aphiwe

The farm was struggling financially so I decided to sell my phone for those cabbages right there, it’s about a hectare.

For Lerato Senakhomo in Nigel, a loan of 72 cattle from the IDC and the Department of Agriculture gave her the momentum to grow her herd. But, it came after two rejected attempts.
Lerato
The first time I applied, I went for an interview and I failed it. I applied again, and failed again. I was so angry. Then on the third attempt,
I got 30 plus 1. Then I tried again and got 72.
She’ll have to pay back her loan, in 42 cows.

What started as a family concern of 2 dairy cows in 2014 is now a sprawling livestock farm.








Lerato

I think at that point in time I had no choice, I had to increase balance sheet.



When we arrive, Senakhomo is taking ownership of some sheep she recently bought.

But her love of farming is truly inspired by her award winning Nguni cattle with their distinctive horns and hide.
Lerato
It can tolerate the heat, it can tolerate cold weather and it’s resistant to many diseases.
Looking at when we arrived here, there was nothing. Now we have trucks, we have cows, we have sheep, we have goats, we have dogs,
The resilience and determination exemplified by Senakhomo and the other farmers we met provide hope for successful land reform. The challenges, though, can’t be underestimated or ignored.




PROMOS
11 Seconds
It’s an age old trade yet its challenges are ever evolving but that’s not stopping young people from changing their careers and getting into farming. Steadily making in roads into the commercial market.

21 Seconds VO UPSOUND
Agriculture is getting a facelift. Young people are pursuing their passion as farmers and they are unphased by its challenges.
As tough as it is, with all it’s difficulties stock theft, lack of funding and high electricity costs and high fuel costs I would never leave my farming, it’s my passion, it’s what I was born to do, it’s what I will die doing.

21 Seconds
The pace of transformation in agriculture has been described as lackluster. But a growing cohort of black farmers are making moves in this industry with minimal support from government or commercial banks.
Keneilwe

If I go to the government, it’s a cry for help, to say I don’t have the security required from the bank. Kindly assist me.
